sections.teaching_text:
1- Translation aka Move:

- Construct a Point.

- Type "Move" and use its component.

- Type "X" and choose "Unit X". So the same for "Y" and "Z".
These are the basic vector directions.

- The INPUT of these basic vectors can used to determine their factor, or length...

- However, sometimes vectors don't have this option available, such as the "Vector XYZ" and "Vector 2pt"
Therefore, the "Amplitude" component works as the factor, or length. The "Amplitude" component needs two INPUTS:
1- Vector
2- Numerical value (to give a length to the vector).

2- Rotation:

- Check out the below "Rotate" components.
They have the same name, however each one has a different function:
- Rotate an object in a plane.
- Rotate an object around an axis.
- Rotate an object in 3D.

Each of these "Rotate" components need different kinds of INPUTS.

- Hover the cursor over the INPUTS and check what they need.

- Using your knowledge in Grasshopper, use each of the three "Rotate" components below to rotate things.

- You can use the "Volume" component to extract the Centroid of the geometry, to be used as the center of Rotation.
Actually in Grasshopper, both the "AREA" & "VOLUME" components provide the respective CENTER & CENTROID of the respective curves and solids, in addition to providing the area and volume.


Rotation Angle: Degree vs. Radian:

- Degrees and Radians are different angle measurement conventions.
- Grasshopper's default angle convention is radians. However, this can be easily switched to degrees if you prefer using degrees...
- Type "Radians" and choose "Radians".
- This component converts the DEGREE INPUT to RADIANS OUTPUT (which can be used to feed the other angular INTPUTS that require RADIANS.
concepts_taught: Rotate an object in a plane.
Rotate an object around an axis.

sections.teaching_text:
3- Planes:

In mathematics, a plane is formed by a minimum of three points.

- Rhino shows the world XYZ planes at the bottom Left of the viewport.
- Make sure to turn the visibility of these guide planes (and the guide axes) on so that you can visually refer to them while working.
Go to:
Tools > Options > Grid
And turn on "Show grid axes" & "Show world axes icon".

The respective colors of the XYZ follow the color convention RGB:
X = Red
Y = Green
Z = Blue

So that when seeing the grid axes, you will notice which axes you are looking at by noticing its color.

You can always turn these grid axes off when needed.

One the uses of planes is the "Mirror" component.
- Type "Mirror" and choose "Mirror".
- Test this component using different planes: XY, YZ, XZ.

There are other ways of constructing and deconstructing planes, as well as other funstions.
You can go to the "Vector" tab, and then "Plane" where you can find many more components.

Change Plane Display:
Display > Preview Plane Size

sections.teaching_text:
5- Surface from Operations: Extrude, Loft, Revolve, etc...

- Surfaces can be made by applying operations.

- Find the below components by either typing inside the Grasshopper workspace or going to the "Surface" tab, then click on "Freeform".
- "Extrude"
- "Loft"
- "Revolve"
- "Pipe"
- "Sweep"


- Hover the cursor over the INPUTS and check what they need.

- Discover the other ways of making surfaces using this method through the "Surface" tab, then click on "Freeform".

sections.teaching_text:
VERY IMPORTANT!

Be careful which components you choose!
Sometimes, components may give the same results visually, but they may have different impacts on the long run, and that could creat problems.

Always double check the result comprehensively in order to avoid problems.

Example below:

Boundary Surface results into a "Trimmed Surface".

Loft results into an "Untrimmed Surface".

Both results work fine. But if you want to make surface divisions, differences are very big and could make you choose which component to beging with!

In this case, Loft works better because in results into an "Untrimmed Surface", which would be a good start for surface division!

sections.teaching_text:
VERY IMPORTANT!

There is not copying in Grasshopper. Transformations are actually copying of geometries.

7- Surface Referencing from Rhino:

- You can always model the surface in Rhino and then reference it inside Grasshopper.

- In Rhino, choose the Surface icon "Surface from 3 or 4 corner points"
- While constructing the surface, start from the bottom left corner and go in a clock-wise fashion.
- After modeling the surface, make sure to make it non-planar.
- Click on the icon "Points on" and move the corner points in Z direction to make a non-planar surface.
- In Grasshopper workspace, type "Surface" and choose "Surface"
- Now select the modeled surface in Rhino, and, inside Grasshopper, right-click on the "Surface" component and select "Set one Surface"


- In case the surface is changed in Rhino, it will automatically update in Grasshopper.
However, if the surface is deleted, the referencing component will become empty and hence the definition will include an error.

- Keep in mind that if there are multiple geometries referenced from Rhino (Points, Lines, Curves, Surfaces, etc...) and few but not all get deleted in Rhino, the Grasshopper referencing component shows an error, however the remaining geometries stay inside the component as referenced.
As a best practice, whenever referenced geometries from Rhino change, it is important to re-reference/update the Grasshopper referencing components and always make sure that the definition does not contain any errors.

additional_teaching_panels.text:
8- Surface Evaluation 1:

Surface Evaluation is finding the properties of a surface at a certain point in space.
For this, we will need to use a point in two different ways!

- Use the component "Contruct Point".
- Keep the X & Z as value 1, and give a number slider to the Y.
- Change the value of the number slider and see where the point is:
1- the point itself in space
2- the point on the evaluated surface

- Now Right-Click on the S INPUT of the "Evaluate Surface" component and select "Reparametrize".
- This will bring the rebuild the domain of the surface to {0;1}:

- If the number slider's range is between 0 & 1, the Point evaluated on the surface will stretch between the beginning and end of the surface's Y side, in the Y direction
- If the number slider's range goes beyond 1, the Point evaluated on the surface will go beyind the surface's Y side, like a factor.
For example, if the number slider is 2, then the Point goes two times the Y side beyond the surface, in the Y direction.

- Use the component "MD Slider".
This is an interesting component since it provides both X & Y information simultaneously. They can be easily changed by manipulating the point on the graph visually.
- Again, "Reparametrize" the S in the "Evaluate Surface" component and make sure to have the domains of both the X & Y of the MD Slider set between {0;1}.

sections.teaching_text:
9- Surface Evaluation 2:

The "Evaluate Surface" component has two interesting OUTPUTS that we will discover now.

1- "P", the resultant Point.
2- "N", the normal at that resultant Point.

- Use the definition that contains the MD Slider,
and use the right combination of the following components to make a line normal to the surface at the resultant point:
- "Move"
- "Amplitude"
- "Number slider"
- "Line"


- Now if you change the MD Slider, you will see that the line normal to the surface changes as well. It moves on the surface and stays always normal to the surface.
- This is possible because every time you change the MD Slider, the resultant "P" changes and also its respective "N", and therefore the Line formed by these resultants changes accordingly.


- An interesting component that shows the local XY Plane at the Point Normal to the Surface is the "Plane Normal".
- Use it in order to show the Plane Normal at the Point evaluated onto the surface. Then change the MD Slider and see how the Plane Normal also changes simultaneously with the Point and the Normal Line.
- To edit the display size of the Plane, go to:
Display > Preview Plane Size

sections.section_title: Surface Transformation: Division, Offset, Flip, Join, etc...
sections.teaching_text:
10- Surface Transformation: Division, Offset, Flip, Join, etc...

- Surfaces can be transformed by many components with various results.
Try the following components and check their INPUTS in order to use them:
- "Divide Surface"
- "Isotrim"
- "Offset"
- "Brep Join"

- To join two surfaces together, we need to use the "Brep Join" component. There is not a "Surface Join" component in Grasshopper since surfaces are also considered as Breps.
A surface is an "open" Brep.
An "open" Brep can also be made out of many surfaces joined together, but not forming a closed solid.
A "closed" Brep is essentially a closed solid object.

additional_teaching_panels.text:
11- Surface Evaluation 3:

Building on the previous "Divide Surface" component, which resulted in many points being applied onto the surface,
Now use these resulting points to make "hair-like" lines normal to the surface.

Hint: use the same combination of components as used before with the single line normal to surface.

sections.teaching_text:
12- Editing the referenced Rhino Surface:

- Select the Rhino surface that is referenced inside Grasshopper.

- Click on "Points On" and change some of the corner points.
You will notice that while doing so, all the Grasshopper parametric geometries update accordingly.

- This is a basic example showing the power of Grasshopper as a Parametric Tool with which you can go back and change something at the beginning of your design process while not losing any of the steps along your Parametric Definition.

- You can even model a totally different surface in Rhino or Grasshopper and then use that new one to feed the Definition from its beginning.

sub_annotations.text:
Assignment 2b:

- Take a look at the "Offset Surface" component & the "Amplitude" of the vector given to make the Normal Lines onto the Surface above.

- Use the same number to both the D INPUT of the "Offset Surface" component and the A INPUT of the "Amplitude" component.

- Turn the visibility of both the resultant offsetted surface and the resultant normal Lines ON.

- Notice that when you change the number slider, the offsetted surface and the Lines changes simultaneously as if they are following each other...

- This is an example of how you can use same numbers with many components' INPUTS.

sections.section_title: We have previously seen how when using the "Evaluate Surface" component with a point of coordinates between 0 and 1, in both X & Y coordinates, the Surface Input would need to be "Reparametrized".
sections.teaching_text:
We have previously seen how when using the "Evaluate Surface" component with a point of coordinates between 0 and 1, in both X & Y coordinates, the Surface Input would need to be "Reparametrized".

However, how can we do that in case the point(s) to be evaluted on the surface are already given, without specific coordinates? Such points may not have coordinates between 0 and 1, which may render reparametrizing the Surface Input pointless.

There is however an interesting component that provides the needed UV Coordinates of points on the Surface (where the Points X & Y are not between 0 & 1) without needing to be reparametrized, the "Surface Closest Point" component.

sub_annotations.text:
IMPORTANT:

The output "UV Point" automatically gives the UV coordinates of all points according to the Surface linked from the input "Surface",

WITHOUT

needing to "Reparametrize" the Surface!
Actually, the "UV Point" already considers the Surface's coordinates, as if it has already been Reparametrized!
sub_annotations.topic: Actually, the "UV Point" already considers the Surface's coordinates, as if it has already been Reparametrized!

sub_annotations.text:
IMPORTANT:

In this case, each surface is "Reparametrized" and evaluated with a Point with X & Y Coordinates between 0 & 1

Since "Surface/Curve" component already provides a "UV Points" output, we can directly use it to evaluate the Point on the Surface.

However, in case such an output is not provided, or if the points comes from Rhino, then we would need to use the "Surface Closest Point" as above
